title: Even with Gemini 3.7 and GPT Luna, AI is completely useless at 3D spatial reasoning for procedural voxel buildings. How is anyone actually making games with this?
author: PumpkinUpstairs
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I've been working on a procedural voxel tech demo with biomes and full physical destruction (inspired by *Teardown*).

To be brutally honest: when it comes to 3D procedural architecture, AI is absolute trash.

I’m not using outdated models, I’ve been testing the latest flagships (Gemini 3.7 and GPT Luna). While they are decent at writing isolated shaders, math helpers, and basic scripts, they completely fall apart the second you ask them to generate or assemble 3D voxel structures.

Even with detailed prompt engineering, step-by-step reasoning, and coordinate constraints, the models constantly output:

* Zero spatial awareness: Rooms with no entrances, doors floating mid-air, stairs leading into solid voxel walls.
* Ugly, disjointed geometry: Slabs that look like random disconnected cardboard boxes rather than cohesive architectural buildings.
* No sense of structural hierarchy: Roofs floating without supports, props clipping inside solid blocks, and total failure at understanding 3D volumetric scale.

It feels like LLMs fundamentally cannot visualize 3D space, coordinate offsets, and spatial grammar.

For those of you who claim to be building real 3D / voxel games with AI:

1. Are you actually having AI generate 3D architecture, or are you manually building 95% of the assets/prefabs in Blender/MagicaVoxel and only using AI for glue code?
2. Is there ANY actual pipeline that works (e.g. 2D floorplan arrays, Wave Function Collapse, strict grammar parsers) to stop the AI from generating deformed geometric garbage?
3. Or is the whole "AI can build 3D procedural worlds" just pure hype that collapses the moment you try to build anything beyond a flat plane?

Would love to hear real, no-BS workflows from people working on complex 3D projects.

TL;DR: Testing Gemini 3.7 and GPT Luna on a procedural Teardown-style voxel demo. Both models are utterly incompetent at 3D spatial reasoning and procedural buildings. How are you guys actually handling 3D voxel generation, or is manual authoring the only real way?

comments.author: CalebKious
comments.body:
I’m building **FateMMO** on a large custom C++ engine. 

It is a 2D MMO rather than a voxel game, but my experience with AI-assisted engine, editor, networking, animation, VFX, and world-content development matches what you are seeing.

The core mistake is asking an LLM to simultaneously act as a level designer, geometry kernel, constraint solver, renderer, and QA system.

An LLM can describe a staircase perfectly, but that does not mean it maintains a persistent internal 3D model of every occupied voxel, clearance volume, doorway, floor transition, support column, and neighboring room. It generates locally plausible decisions. Architecture requires global invariants that remain valid after thousands of dependent decisions.

That is why you repeatedly get:  
Individually reasonable pieces that do not form a coherent building.  
Coordinate drift as the structure grows.  
Doors and stairs that satisfy the prompt locally but violate the surrounding occupancy grid.  
Rooms that exist geometrically but are unreachable.  
Decorative details placed before circulation and structural requirements are solved.  
Code that runs correctly while producing a semantically broken result.

AI does not fail because it has never heard of doors or stairs. It fails because nothing deterministic is enforcing what a valid door or staircase must connect.

In my FateMMO work, AI has been most valuable when it operates **inside systems that already have hard rules and feedback**. It can help implement an ECS system, networking feature, editor tool, shader, animation controller, serializer, test suite, or data pipeline because the compiler, tests, protocol, renderer, and runtime expose whether the work is valid. It becomes much less reliable when asked to invent a large interconnected system with no authoritative representation or validator.

For voxel architecture, I would not have the model generate raw structures or thousands of voxel coordinates. I would use something closer to this pipeline:  
Manually create a constrained modular kit: walls, corners, doors, windows, stairs, shafts, roof pieces, supports, props, and destruction variants. Every module gets dimensions, connection sockets, clearance volumes, semantic tags, and placement rules.  
Have the AI generate only a high-level building specification: footprint, floor count, room types, approximate dimensions, adjacency requirements, entrances, vertical circulation, architectural style, and density.  
Convert that specification into a room graph. Before creating any geometry, validate that every required room is connected and that the graph contains valid paths from each floor to an exit.  
Use deterministic generation for the actual layout: BSP, shape grammars, constraint propagation, Wave Function Collapse, backtracking, or a custom solver. The AI can select parameters and rules, but it should not be the final authority on placement.  
Reserve stairwells, elevator shafts, entrances, support lines, and utility corridors before subdividing the remaining floor area. Vertical circulation has to be solved across all floors together, not added afterward.  
Compile the accepted floorplan into voxel geometry using known templates. Walls, roofs, doors, and stairs should be produced by code that cannot create an invalid orientation or unsupported connection.  
Run automated validation after generation: flood-fill reachability, doorway connectivity, stair landing clearance, overlap checks, minimum corridor width, ceiling clearance, roof coverage, support checks, prop intersections, and navmesh connectivity.  
Reject or repair failed layouts. Give the AI the validator output—such as “second floor bedroom is unreachable” or “stair volume intersects exterior wall”—rather than asking it to visually guess what went wrong.

For a destruction-heavy game, I would also separate the structure into semantic layers. Generate a valid circulation and structural skeleton first, then add destructible walls, facade pieces, furniture, and debris around it. Every component should know whether it is structural, decorative, traversable, destructible, or required for progression. Otherwise destruction and generation will compound each other’s failures.

A 2D floorplan-first approach is probably the strongest workaround. Generate each floor as a constrained occupancy grid, but solve all vertical connectors globally. Once the floorplans pass connectivity and clearance tests, extrude them into 3D and apply facade and roof grammars. This removes most of the free-form 3D reasoning from the AI.

AI is genuinely useful for:  
Writing and maintaining the procedural-generation framework.  
Producing shaders, VFX logic, destruction helpers, editor tooling, and debug visualizations.  
Designing schemas, grammars, validation rules, and automated tests.  
Generating variations from approved templates.  
Selecting themes, room programs, materials, prop sets, and generation parameters.  
Analyzing failed seeds, logs, screenshots, and validator output.  
Creating concept art and references for human-authored modular assets.  
Automating repetitive content-authoring work.  
It is currently much worse at being the unconstrained final author of spatially coherent production environments.

So my answer to your three questions would be:  
**1.** For a serious project, I would expect most dependable geometry and modules to remain human-authored or deterministically generated. AI can control composition, but it should not freely invent every voxel.  
**2.** Yes, workable pipelines exist, but the success comes from floorplan graphs, modular sockets, WFC or grammar systems, constraint solvers, and aggressive validation—not from better prompting alone.  
**3.** “AI autonomously builds complete, coherent 3D worlds from a prompt” is mostly hype when no deterministic framework exists underneath it. “AI accelerates the creation of a procedural world system and supplies constrained high-level plans” is absolutely real.

The practical rule I have learned from FateMMO is: **let AI propose; let deterministic systems construct and verify.** The more of the result that can be compiled, simulated, tested, or rejected automatically, the more useful AI becomes.

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
1.) Like 3D AI generators I generate 2D images (front, top, side) then feed these to the AI with my request. When done I use Gaussian Splatting. Alternatively I use an 3D AI generator.

2.) No. This is the problem with AI, it needs huge amounts of data to be exact. Instead we depend on **tolerance**. For example when you ask for an image of an sun set, you have an high tolerance, *any* image of an sunset looks good. 

However if you ask it for an sunset in an France an specific street it will have too little data, and probably just plant the Eiffel Tower in the image.

3.) It is not Hype, you can train AI on 3D worlds then it can generate 3D worlds. The problem is you need tons of data. It is easier to generate 3D from 2D.

You must understand, AI is not an Genie, it is not an Laborer or an Entity. It can't do work, it can only make an prediction based on it's data. So ask the AI for simple tasks "generate an valley" and edit it, or ask it for things that there are tons of data on "Valley of the Ten Peaks".

Mostly, provide as much data as you can, don't depend on one AI.

comments.author: Low-Cook-3544
comments.body:
just ask for a custom debug view with coordinates right as you start building your game. you can activate this at any point and direct the spatial perception as you wish. 

then you can set up self-optimizing harnesses or guides for the model to read at any point before doing another 3d overhaul. get it to read the guide -> implement the changes -> note down what bugs you ask to be fixed -> update its own guide so that such issues don't occur again. this helps when you reach context limits/context compression whether you're building directly in a terminal of a vibe coding app
